title: When the Cellar Breaks
premise: Folklorist Yara Okafor arrives in the dying village of Hollowmere to record a harvest song that locals will sing once but never twice, and discovers that every photograph from her late grandmother's house now contains an extra empty chair. The chair is an invitation: the cellar beneath the house opens each harvest season to collect those who belong, and Yara's grandmother spent her life keeping her family out of its ledger by never finishing the song's last verse. As the harvest moon waxes, Yara — who has never believed and refuses to start — must learn the final verse from the village's last willing singer without ever singing along herself, because singing it completes the invitation. In the climax she enters the cellar to retrieve her cousin Tobi, who sang along by accident, and breaks the cycle not by refusing the song but by giving the cellar what it truly wanted: to be remembered, sung about, and then let go. The book ends with Yara recording the whole song for the first time, the photographs restored to their true count, and one chair left deliberately empty at the table — belonging, finally, chosen rather than claimed.
about_author: Wendell Coldharbour is the pen name of a former archivist of regional folk music collections who spent a decade cataloguing songs no community would perform twice. They write horror about the places where memory becomes architecture.

chapters.title: The Song They Sing Once
chapters.summary: Yara Okafor arrives in Hollowmere with recording equipment and professional skepticism, interviewing villagers about a harvest song everyone knows and no one will repeat. Old Marta sings it once, flawlessly, then goes pale and asks Yara to leave. POV: Yara. Beat: curiosity sharpening into unease as the village's silence reveals itself as discipline, not ignorance.

chapters.title: Grandmother's House
chapters.summary: Yara inherits temporary custody of her grandmother Edith's house on the village edge and begins cataloguing Edith's own folklore papers, finding decades of notes on the same song — all ending mid-verse. POV: Yara. Beat: grief braided with scholarly excitement; the house feels expectant, like a held breath.

chapters.title: One Chair Too Many
chapters.summary: Sorting family photographs, Yara notices an extra wooden chair in every image spanning forty years — always empty, always slightly closer to the camera in later photos. Her cousin Tobi laughs it off; the village shopkeeper does not laugh at all. POV: Yara. Beat: the first hard crack in her unbelief, rendered as denial doubling down.

chapters.title: What the Cellar Keeps
chapters.summary: Yara explores the locked cellar and finds it larger than the house above: shelves of shoes, coats, a child's drawing signed with her mother's name. The door closes behind her without being touched. POV: Yara. Beat: dread arriving through detail rather than spectacle; she leaves and tells no one.

chapters.title: Tobi Hums It
chapters.summary: Tobi, visiting for the summer, catches the melody from Yara's recordings and hums it while washing dishes — and every clock in the house stops for exactly one verse-length of time. Yara deletes the files; the humming continues anyway. POV: alternating Yara and Tobi. Beat: protective panic; the mistake has already been made.

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Following Edith's notes, Yara pries up the kitchen floor and finds a handwritten ledger listing names by year — including Edith's sister, crossed out, and two blank lines dated this harvest. One line has begun filling itself in: T-O-B. POV: Yara. Beat: cold clarity; belief is no longer optional, only strategy.

chapters.title: Marta's Price
chapters.summary: Yara begs old Marta to teach her the last verse. Marta agrees to explain why she can't: fifty years ago she sang it twice, and her brother walked into the cellar smiling. She'll trade knowledge for a promise Yara isn't sure she can keep. POV: Marta, framed within Yara's interview recordings. Beat: sorrow as inheritance; the village's cruelty is really grief wearing armor.

chapters.title: Rules of the Verse
chapters.summary: Through three nights of lessons, Marta teaches everything except the melody itself: listen, mouth it, never voice it. Yara learns the verse describes the cellar as a hungry guest who only wants a seat at the table. POV: Yara. Beat: found-family warmth flickering between the two women, fragile as dry kindling.

chapters.title: The Chair Moves
chapters.summary: The extra chair in the photographs now sits at the head of the table, and in the newest picture — taken yesterday, by no one — Tobi sits beside it, mid-laugh. Yara realizes the cellar isn't luring them; it's rehearsing them. POV: Tobi. Beat: violation of the self; Tobi begins losing hours and finding mud on his shoes.

chapters.title: Village of the Twice-Silent
chapters.summary: Yara confronts the village council, who admit the truth they've managed for generations: the cellar takes one per harvest unless fed with songs sung about it, never with it. Half want Yara gone before she ruins the arrangement. POV: Yara. Beat: anger at complicity; belonging revealed as something the village bought with other people's children.

chapters.title: Edith's Unfinished Letter
chapters.summary: In Edith's papers Yara finds a letter addressed to 'whoever hears the verse' explaining that Edith kept the last verse incomplete on purpose — a locked door needs no key if you never build the handle. But the letter ends: 'the cellar learns. It has started writing its own.' POV: Yara. Beat: dread recontextualized; the enemy is patient and literate.

chapters.title: Night of the Waxing Moon
chapters.summary: With the moon half-full, the house begins singing the last verse itself — walls, pipes, floorboards harmonizing in Edith's voice. Tobi sleepwalks toward the cellar door; Yara holds him back until dawn, hands bleeding on the handle. POV: alternating. Beat: exhaustion and tenderness; Yara's found family is now just one boy and a dead woman's voice.

chapters.title: The Singer Who Remembers
chapters.summary: Yara seeks out Ivo, a hollow-eyed man the village pretends not to see — the only person who ever heard the complete verse and survived, because he was in the cellar when it was sung. He offers to teach it, for a price paid in memories. POV: Ivo. Beat: pity curdling into fear; memory as currency, foreshadowing the theme's cost.

chapters.title: Paid in Remembering
chapters.summary: Ivo teaches Yara the melody note by note while taking pieces of her past in exchange — her mother's face, her university years, the smell of her childhood kitchen. She writes everything down frantically, knowing the notes are next. POV: Yara. Beat: grief for a self being sold off; the theme of memory made literal and terrible.

chapters.title: The Verse With No Handle
chapters.summary: Yara has the full verse memorized but unsung, and discovers Ivo's secret: he survives because the cellar keeps him as its memory, unable to die or leave. He begs her to finish what Edith started — not lock the door, but close the house forever. POV: Ivo. Beat: moral weight transferred; the plan requires sacrifice Yara hasn't agreed to.

chapters.title: Tobi Sings
chapters.summary: On the night before the harvest moon, Tobi — half-gone already, dreaming in the cellar's rhythm — sings the last verse aloud, complete and clear. The ledger's second blank line begins to fill. The house exhales. POV: Tobi. Beat: heartbreak and helplessness; the accident the whole structure feared has happened.

chapters.title: Down the Stairs That Weren't There
chapters.summary: The cellar door stands open onto stairs descending farther than physics allows. Yara, armed with the unsung verse and Edith's letter, goes down after Tobi as the harvest moon rises over Hollowmere. POV: Yara. Beat: resolve replacing terror; she descends not believing she'll win, only that she won't abandon him.

chapters.title: The Table Below
chapters.summary: In the deep cellar Yara finds a long table set for a feast, generations of the taken seated and smiling, Tobi newly placed among them, and at the head — the chair from the photographs, finally occupied by something shaped like patience. It speaks in Edith's voice: it only ever wanted to belong. POV: Yara. Beat: horror pivoting to terrible empathy; the monster's motive is loneliness.

chapters.title: Sung About, Never With
chapters.summary: Yara understands the bargain's flaw: the cellar was excluded from every song, remembered only as hunger. She stands at the table and sings the complete verse — about the cellar, naming it, grieving it — without inviting it, turning the song from summons to elegy. The seated generations stir. POV: Yara. Beat: climax; the theme of belonging answered with inclusion instead of refusal.

chapters.title: Letting Go of the Table
chapters.summary: The cellar, named and mourned at last, loosens its grip: the guests stand, thank it, and dissolve upward like smoke remembering their shapes. Tobi wakes weeping in Yara's arms. The thing in the chair bows its head and asks, small, whether anyone will sing of it tomorrow. Yara promises. POV: Yara. Beat: catharsis; release achieved through witness, not exorcism.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair We Keep
chapters.summary: Above ground, the photographs return to their true counts except one — where the chair remains, now clearly a memorial rather than a lure. The village, shaken, gathers to hear Yara play the full recording aloud, the first time in living memory the song is sung twice, safely, together. POV: Yara. Beat: communal healing; belonging rebuilt on honesty instead of fear.

chapters.title: Last Verse, First Recording
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Yara finishes cataloguing Edith's papers, adds her own final entry, and mails copies of the recording to archives across the country so the cellar can never be forgotten again — or need to take anyone. At the table, she sets one empty place, out of love. POV: Yara. Beat: quiet resolution; memory preserved freely is the difference between a haunting and a heritage.
